extra.message: Hardcoded Django SECRET_KEY in Source Code — Session forgery and hijacking, CSRF token forgery, cryptographic signature bypass, cookie tampering, potential remote code execution via pickle deserialization if combined with other vulnerabilities [verified: SECRET_KEY is a literal hardcoded string at settings.py line 90 committed to the repository; no environment variable, external secrets manager, or key rotation mechanism is referenced anywhere in the codebase, enabling cryptographic forgery of sessions and signed tokens.]

Remote Code Execution via exec() on User Input — Full arbitrary Python code execution on the server; attacker can read/write files, exfiltrate data, install backdoors, pivot to internal network [verified: User-supplied POST parameter 'first_name' is base64-decoded and passed directly to exec() at line 72 with no validation, sanitization, or sandboxing; a second exec path at line 76 provides a Python 2 fallback.]

Arbitrary Python Code Execution via exec() — Remote code execution on the server — full system compromise, data exfiltration, lateral movement. [verified: Same code path as finding 0: user-supplied POST input is base64-decoded and passed to exec() at line 72 with no controls, enabling full arbitrary Python code execution.]

DEBUG=True Enabled Exposing Stack Traces and Internals — Information disclosure of application structure, file paths, variable values, configuration details, and potentially secrets from stack traces; aids reconnaissance for further attacks [verified: DEBUG=True is set at settings.py line 10 and the /misconfiguration/boom endpoint raises an unhandled exception at views.py line 144, guaranteeing full stack traces with local variables, settings, and file paths are exposed to any anonymous user.]

DEBUG=True Exposes Stack Traces and Settings — Information disclosure — stack traces reveal code paths, file locations, and configuration; combined with the boom endpoint, attackers can trivially trigger and view full diagnostic pages. [verified: Same DEBUG=True finding as finding 1: DEBUG is True at settings.py line 10 and the boom view at views.py line 144 makes stack traces trivially triggerable by any unauthenticated user.]

CSRF Protection Disabled Globally — Attackers can forge cross-site requests that perform state-changing actions on behalf of victims; all POST endpoints are exploitable including code execution and user profile modification [verified: CsrfViewMiddleware is commented out at settings.py line 102, no {% csrf_token %} appears in any POST form template (gift_card.html, profile.html, sql.html, code_execution.html), and no alternative CSRF protection (custom middleware, SameSite cookies, origin validation) exists anywhere in the codebase.]

CSRF Protection Globally Disabled — Cross-site request forgery on all state-changing endpoints — unauthorized data modification, privilege escalation, and transaction forgery. [verified: Same CSRF middleware gap as finding 0: CsrfViewMiddleware is commented out at settings.py line 102, all POST forms lack csrf_token, and no alternative origin validation exists.]

Debug Toolbar Accessible via Query Parameter — Exposure of application internals including template contexts, request/response data, settings, cache contents, and session data; significantly aids further attacks [verified: The show_toolbar callback at settings.py lines 180-183 returns True for any truthy ?debug= query parameter with no authentication, IP restriction, or admin check, making the full debug toolbar (SQL, templates, settings, cache) accessible to anyone.]

Debug Toolbar Exposed via User-Controlled Query Parameter — Severe information leakage — database query details, configuration variables, application internals, and software versions all disclosed to any unauthenticated user. [verified: Same debug toolbar exposure as finding 3: the show_toolbar callback at settings.py lines 180-183 unconditionally enables the toolbar for any request with ?debug=1 with no access control whatsoever.]

Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Read — Arbitrary file read on the server; exposure of SECRET_KEY, source code, configuration, system files such as /etc/passwd [verified: The 'p' GET parameter is used directly in os.path.join(base_path, filename) at line 42 and then opened with open(); no path validation, whitelist, or rejection of '..' or '/' exists, and the error messages even hint at path traversal.]

Arbitrary Function Dispatch via globals() Lookup — Bypass of access controls, unauthorized access to admin functionality, ability to invoke any module-level function including those with dangerous side effects [verified: The 'fwd' GET parameter is looked up in globals() at line 183 and called directly; an attacker can supply 'admin' or 'code_execution' to invoke privileged or dangerous functions without any authorization.]

Arbitrary Function Dispatch via globals() — Privilege escalation to admin functions, unauthorized code path execution, and potential RCE via chaining to other dangerous functions. [verified: Same code path as finding 5: the 'fwd' GET parameter is resolved via globals().get(forward) at line 183 and called with no restriction on which functions can be dispatched.]

Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) — Unauthorized access to other users' profiles including name, email, and admin status; ability to modify other users' data via POST without authentication [verified: users.get(userid) at line 130 performs no authentication or authorization check; any anonymous user can access any user profile and POST to lines 132-135 to modify another user's name and email.]

Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) — Unauthorized access to other users' profiles and data, discovery of admin users, modification of other users' name and email fields. [verified: Same code path as finding 2: users.get(userid) at line 130 lacks any ownership or authorization check, allowing any user to view and POST-modify other users' profiles.]

Deliberate Exception Endpoint Leaks Stack Trace — Information disclosure — full Django diagnostic page with stack trace, local variables, and configuration exposed to any anonymous user. [verified: The boom view at line 144 unconditionally raises Exception('boom'), and with DEBUG=True (settings.py line 14), Django returns full diagnostic pages with stack traces and configuration to any anonymous visitor.]

Missing Function-Level Access Control via Query String — Unauthorized access to admin interface; privilege escalation from anonymous user to admin by manipulating a query parameter [verified: The admin check at line 157 is solely request.GET.get('action') == 'admin' with no real authentication mechanism; any user can append ?action=admin to bypass.]

Open Redirect via User-Supplied URL — Phishing attacks redirecting users to attacker-controlled sites that mimic the legitimate application; malware distribution; bypass of security controls [verified: request.GET.get('url') is passed directly to Django's redirect() at line 178 with no validation or whitelist, enabling phishing redirects to any external domain.]

Missing Clickjacking Protection (X-Frame-Options) — Clickjacking attacks where users are tricked into clicking hidden UI elements on the application when embedded in an attacker's iframe; potential CSRF amplification [verified: XFrameOptionsMiddleware is commented out at settings.py line 106 and no custom X-Frame-Options header is set via any other mechanism, but the app lacks authentication so clickjacking provides no privilege escalation beyond the already-missing CSRF protection.]

Insecure Session Cookie Configuration — Session cookies can be stolen via network sniffing (no Secure flag), via XSS (no HttpOnly flag), and sent in cross-site requests (no SameSite); enables session hijacking [verified: No SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE, SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY, or SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE are configured anywhere in settings.py, but the application has no authentication and sessions carry no sensitive state, limiting real-world impact to a defense-in-depth gap.]

Monster Cookie Set Without Secure or HttpOnly Flags — Cookie accessible to JavaScript (no HttpOnly) enabling theft via existing XSS vulnerabilities; transmitted over unencrypted connections (no Secure) enabling network sniffing [verified: response.set_cookie() at line 100 omits httponly, secure, and samesite flags, but the cookie value 'omnomnomnomnom!' is a harmless dummy string containing no real secrets or session data.]

Cookie Set Without Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite Flags — Cookie accessible via JavaScript (XSS), transmittable over unencrypted HTTP, and vulnerable to cross-site request inclusion. [verified: Same code as finding 6: the monster cookie at line 100 is set without security flags, but the value is a harmless dummy string with no sensitive content.]
